summary:
Huánuco stands under Peru's national framework: Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The facilities restriction is national in scope. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering or using a public sanitary facility designated for the sex other than their birth sex. The text carries narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where entry is required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and it obliges venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. At the time of that committee vote the text still required plenary backing. The reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes, whose Article 5.1 bars entry to public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than the person's birth sex. The provision binds trans people, including trans youth, to facilities that do not match their gender identity, and the same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Enforcement reaches everyday spaces. Activist Gianna Camacho has argued that the restriction would be applied by security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. A consumer-protection body has already applied the logic in a private setting: SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, which based restroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia counted 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; among the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and the perpetrators were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023. Peru has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

Document and identity recognition remain a constraint: gender-identity recognition in Peru is a process that is long, costly and invasive.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5.1 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. IDEHPUCP has also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
localsOnly:
Residents of Huánuco who seek legal recognition of their gender identity face a process that IDEHPUCP characterises as long, costly and invasive, with no streamlined route documented in the sources reviewed.

A discrimination complaint may be lodged with the national consumer-protection body, but its record is unfavourable to trans complainants on facilities: SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's case against SmartFit after the gym relied on the sex recorded in the DNI. Whether a complaint brought from Huánuco would be assessed differently is not sourced.

Residents prosecuted for violence against a trans person cannot be charged under hate-crime provisions, since the Penal Code's LGBT coverage was removed in 2017 and sexual orientation and gender identity are absent from the state's crime-registration systems. Reporting a killing of a trans person therefore enters the record as an ordinary homicide, which is one reason the observatory's counts are described as a sub-registry.

Healthcare settings in the country changed their official terminology in June 2024, removing pathologising language for gender diversity, which affects how trans patients are documented and treated by providers.
outOfScopeNotes:
All three sources reviewed are national in scope and none contains Huánuco-specific content; the department's position is therefore scored against the national framework rather than against local reporting. Whether venues, hospitals or police stations in Huánuco enforce the restroom restriction, and whether the province or any district has its own anti-discrimination or facilities ordinance, is unresolved and not sourced here.

No Huánuco-specific record of violence against trans people appears in the inventory. The national homicide and rights-violation totals are attributed to the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia and cover 2020 to 2023; no subnational breakdown by department is provided, so the distribution of those killings, including any in Huánuco, remains unresolved.

Whether the July 2023 airport restroom complaint or any subsequent enforcement action has produced litigation or an administrative decision in Huánuco is not sourced. The one consumer-protection decision cited, Resolution 0735-2022, concerns a private gym chain and is reported without a department.

The sources do not state whether trans visitors entering Peru can obtain or amend a DNI reflecting their gender identity before or after arrival, and they do not address entry, visa or customs screening for trans travellers.
